blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette
stem: Which instruction is part of respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette in a healthcare setting?

options.A: Cover the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing, discard used tissues, and perform hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions.
options.B: Use a tissue for coughing or sneezing, then keep the tissue for repeated use during the visit if visible contamination is limited.
options.C: Cover coughs and sneezes with the hands, then rely on gloves during the visit instead of performing hand hygiene after secretions contact.
options.D: Perform hand hygiene after coughing or sneezing only when no tissue was used, because proper tissue use removes the need for hand cleaning.

rationale: A is correct. CDC respiratory-hygiene guidance instructs people with respiratory symptoms to cover the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing, use and dispose of tissues, and perform hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions or contaminated materials. B is incorrect because used tissues should be discarded. C is incorrect because cough etiquette does not replace hand hygiene and hands should not be used as the preferred cough barrier. D is incorrect because hand hygiene is recommended after contact with respiratory secretions even when tissues are used.
educational_objective: Apply respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette by covering coughs and sneezes, disposing of tissues, and performing hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_document_title: Respiratory Hygiene/Cough Etiquette; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: Current CDC respiratory-hygiene resources live-rechecked 2026-08-21; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: CDC respiratory-hygiene/cough-etiquette guidance: cover mouth/nose with a tissue when coughing or sneezing, dispose of used tissue in the nearest receptacle, and perform hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions and contaminated objects/materials.
source_claim_supported: Current CDC guidance directly supports cough/sneeze covering, disposal of used tissues, and hand hygiene after respiratory-secretions contact.

option_audit.B: Plausible conservation shortcut but incorrect because used tissues should be discarded.
option_audit.C: Plausible barrier substitution but incorrect because respiratory etiquette does not eliminate hand hygiene and hands are not the preferred cough barrier.
option_audit.D: Plausible misunderstanding of tissue use but incorrect because hand hygiene follows respiratory-secretions contact even when tissues are used.
